title: Longitudinal Assessment of EGFR and MET Transcriptional Activity Using Cell-Free Chromatin Immunoprecipitation in Two Patients with EGFR-Mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Background/Objectives: MET amplification represents the most common bypass resistance mechanism to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) treatment in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Combination therapy with the EGFR-TKI, osimertinib, and the MET-TKI, crizotinib, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in overcoming this resistance.
However, assessing MET transcriptional activity during treatment remains challenging.

Methods: Cell-free chromatin immunoprecipitation (cfChIP) targeting H3 lysine 36 trimethylation (H3K36me3) was employed to investigate the transcriptional activity of the EGFR and MET genes in serial liquid biopsies obtained from two patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC.
Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) was used to quantify circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and cfChIP enrichment levels.

Results: In PT1, H3K36me3 m EGFR and MET cfChIP enrichment increased during disease progression, with MET enrichment increasing further following the initiation of crizotinib/osimertinib combination therapy, during which the patient experienced a partial response.
In PT2, MET amplification was detected in a liquid biopsy, but MET cfChIP enrichment remained low throughout the treatment course, and the patient did not respond to crizotinib.
Conclusions: This two-patient feasibility study illustrates the potential of cfChIP-ddPCR for the longitudinal assessment of EGFR and MET transcriptional activity in liquid biopsies.
These observations warrant further investigation of cfChIP as an approach for monitoring transcriptional activity during osimertinib/crizotinib treatment.

body.text: Lung cancer, with 2.5 million new cases and 1.8 million deaths reported in 2022, remains the leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality [,].
Lung cancer is broadly classified into small cell lung cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the latter being the most common form, accounting for 85% of cases [].
Adenocarcinoma is the most frequent NSCLC subtype and approximately 12-17% harbor activating mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) [,].
The most common activating mutations include in-frame deletions of exon 19 (ex19del) and the L858R mutation in exon 21 [].
Osimertinib, the third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI), is the standard first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC in most countries [,].
However, acquired resistance is inevitable, with MET amplification being the most common EGFR bypass mechanism [].
This has led to combination therapy with osimertinib and novel MET-TKIs, such as savolitinib, with promising results in early-phase clinical studies [,,].
Crizotinib, which inhibits MET among other kinases, has also demonstrated benefit in some case studies [,].
However, treatment response to MET-TKIs appears to differ between patients, underscoring the need to identify predictive biomarkers.

Minimally invasive liquid biopsies are widely investigated, as they allow longitudinal disease monitoring through repeated sampling without the complications and patient discomfort associated with traditional tissue biopsies [,,,,,].

From a blood sample, tumor-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA), referred to as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), provides information on tumor genetics in cancer patients [,]. ctDNA has emerged as a biomarker in EGFR-positive NSCLC to track tumor burden and predict both TKI response and disease [,].

Clearance of ctDNA during osimertinib treatment has been associated with early response leading to longer progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS), whereas elevated EGFR mutant allele frequency (MAF) has been associated with disease progression [,].

The utility of ctDNA as a biomarker has primarily been confined to the detection of gene alterations, but recent technological advancements have enabled the ability to detect the epigenetic properties of cfDNA [].

Cell-free chromatin immunoprecipitation (cfChIP) utilizes post-translational histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in the bloodstream and reflects gene expression in the cell from which it originated [,,].

This includes the trimethylation of lysine 36 on histone H3 (H3K36me3), which is associated with active gene transcription [,,,]. cfChIP targeting H3K36me3 enables the selective immunoprecipitation of cell-free nucleosomes in plasma bearing this modification, thereby reflecting transcriptionally active genes.

Previously, our lab demonstrated that H3K36me3-cfChIP followed by droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) quantification results in the enrichment of mutant EGFR fragments compared to EGFR wild type, consistent with the active transcription of the EGFR mutant allele in the tumor [].

In this study, we expanded the application of the cfChIP methodology to longitudinally monitor the transcriptional activity of mutant EGFR (mEGFR) and MET in patients treated with osimertinib and crizotinib.
The aim of this proof-of-concept study was to explore the feasibility of using cfChIP to assess gene-associated transcriptional activity longitudinally in patients treated with osimertinib.
The observations provide a rationale for further investigation of the approach in larger prospective studies.
The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Central Denmark Region Committee on Biomedical Research Ethics (No. 1-16-02-211-16).
Informed consent was obtained from all individuals involved in the study.
The included patients were diagnosed with stage IV EGFR-mutated NSCLC and received first-line osimertinib therapy.
The patients developed resistance through MET amplification after which they received crizotinib/osimertinib combination therapy.
Serial blood samples were collected before and after initiation of the combination therapy.
Peripheral blood was collected into Streck or EDTA-containing tubes and centrifuged within 2 h at 1400 g for 15 min at room temperature.
Aliquoted plasma was stored at -80 °C until use.
Cell-free DNA was purified from plasma using the AVENIO cfDNA Isolation Kit (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) and sequenced using the AVENIO ctDNA Surveillance Kit (Roche).
The next-generation sequencing (NGS) library was sequenced using a NextSeq 500 and data were processed using the AVENIO Oncology Analysis Software v.
For this study, we only focused on the detection of MET amplification, which was defined as a CNV score > 5.
cfChIP was executed as outlined in Maansson et al. [].

Briefly, plasma was cleared of circulating antibodies using empty protein A/G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and subsequently mixed with anti-H3K36me3-coated protein A/G magnetic beads followed by incubation O/N at 4 °C.
Beads were washed and precipitated DNA was eluted. cfChIP samples were purified using the Apostle MiniMax High Efficiency cfDNA Isolation kit (Apostle Bio, Pleasanton, CA, USA).
Input cfDNA samples were purified with the Apostle MiniMax High Efficiency cfDNA Isolation kit or the AVENIO ctDNA Isolation Kit V2 (Roche).

The study uses ChIP and input DNA samples extracted from the lung adenocarcinoma cell lines, including parental HCC827 (RRID: CVCL_2063, ATCC, LCG Standards, Wesel, Germany), its MET-amplified subclone (HCC827-MET) described in [], and A549 (RRID: CVCL_0023, ATCC, LCG Standards).
Cell culture, chromatin isolation, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and DNA purification were all performed as described by Maansson et al. [].

Droplet digital PCR was performed using the QX200 AutoDG Droplet Digital PCR System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) and Bio-Rad’s mutation assays for EGFR E19del (Bio-Rad, Assay ID dHsaMVD2010039) and MET WT (Bio-Rad, Assay ID dHsaIS2503879, Table A1).
The MET WT assay was supplied as part of a duplex assay containing primer/probe sets for both wild-type and mutant MET.
However, only the wild-type MET assay was used for the analyses presented in this study.

The experiments were run in duplicates where each well contained 11 ddPCR supermix for probes (no dUTP), 1 μL of each primer (Table A2) and probe (Table A3) and 5-10 μL cfChIP or input sample for a total volume of 22 μL.

Droplets were generated using the QX200 automated droplet generator (Bio-Rad) and PCR amplification was performed on a thermocycler (Eppendorf SE, Hamburg, Germany) with the following setup: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min, 40 PCR cycles of 30 s denaturation at 94 °C and 1 min annealing at 55 °C or 58 °C, 10 min at 98 °C followed by rest at 4 °C O/N.
Droplets were read using the QX200 Droplet Reader (Bio-Rad) and data were analyzed using Bio-Rad’s QuantasoftTM software version 1.7.4.
Non-template controls containing HyPure water were used to establish the threshold for positive droplets.
Mutant allele frequencies were calculated as the number of droplets positive for the mutant variant compared to the total number of WT and variant positive droplets.

ChIP enrichment was estimated by counting the number of positive cfChIP droplets and adjusting for differences in plasma used for cfChIP, elution volumes and sample volumes used for ddPCR. cfChIP enrichment was used as a measure of the total transcriptional activity of the target gene, irrespective of whether this activity resulted from increased transcription per gene copy or from gene amplification.
Accordingly, cfChIP enrichment was not adjusted for gene copy number.
The first patient (PT1, Figure 1 top) was a 29-year-old woman, never-smoker with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, carrying a germline TP53 mutation, predisposing to multiple cancers [].
She was diagnosed with stage IV EGFR-ex19del-mutated NSCLC with liver and bone metastases.

First-line osimertinib induced a response for two years, after which progression was treated with chemotherapy (carboplatin/pemetrexed) in combination with osimertinib, resulting in a further six-month response.
At subsequent progression, MET amplification was detected in both liquid and tissue biopsies from a new liver metastasis.
Crizotinib was therefore added to osimertinib, resulting in a response in all tumor lesions within one month.
The second patient (PT2, Figure 1 bottom) was a 36-year-old never-smoker with stage IV EGFR-ex19del-mutated NSCLC with liver, bone, and brain metastases.
First-line osimertinib induced a response for nearly 1.5 years.
At 16 months, progression was observed in a single liver metastasis, with MET amplification detected in a liquid biopsy.
EGFR-ex19del was confirmed in the liver metastasis, but no additional genetic alterations were identified.
Crizotinib was subsequently added to continued osimertinib treatment, but the patient showed continuous disease progression and no response to the combination.
Crizotinib was discontinued, and treatment was changed to radiotherapy and chemotherapy (carboplatin/vinorelbine) while osimertinib was continued, resulting in a partial response within two months.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Both patients received osimertinib and subsequently had MET amplification detected in liquid biopsies.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: We therefore assessed EGFR and MET cfChIP enrichment longitudinally to characterize gene-associated transcriptional activity during their treatment courses.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: We developed ChIP-ddPCR assays to quantify EGFR and MET gene activity and validated them in multiple cell lines (see Figure A1 and Figure A2, Appendix A).

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: H3K36me3 cfChIP-ddPCR was performed on longitudinal plasma samples from PT1 and PT2.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: To confirm that cfChIP enrichment reflected gene activity in the cells of origin, we quantified the active gene ACTG1 and the lowly expressed gene DNAJC5G (Figure 2A).

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Blood cells are the primary source of cfDNA [] and show high ACTG1 but low DNAJC5G expression (Figure A3).

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Consistent with this, ACTG1 showed clear cfChIP enrichment (Figure 2B), demonstrating that cfChIP can detect transcriptionally active genes in plasma.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: To assess EGFR and MET gene-associated transcriptional activity, we quantified mEGFR and MET cfChIP enrichment in serial plasma samples.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Before first-line osimertinib, PT1 had a high ctDNA fraction, reflected by an EGFR MAF of 54.9% (Figure 3A), and mEGFR showed 1.5-fold higher cfChIP enrichment than ACTG1.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Following osimertinib treatment, mEGFR became undetectable in the plasma and cfChIP samples, coinciding with partial response (PR).

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: At progression (22 months), mEGFR reappeared in plasma, while subsequent chemotherapy reduced the ctDNA levels.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: At the second progression (30 months), mEGFR cfChIP enrichment increased to 1.2-fold relative to ACTG1, accompanied by an EGFR MAF of 32.5%.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: At this time, MET amplification was detected and MET cfChIP enrichment increased to 2.1-fold relative to ACTG1, corresponding to a 6.7-fold increase in MET enrichment compared with baseline.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Following the addition of crizotinib to osimertinib, MET cfChIP enrichment increased further to 3.3-fold relative to ACTG1 (32 months), while mEGFR enrichment and EGFR MAF decreased to 4.3%, coinciding with radiological PR.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Subsequent samples showed declining ctDNA levels, low mEGFR MAF, and reduced MET enrichment.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: In PT2, partial response to osimertinib after four months was reflected by a low mEGFR MAF of 0.4% (Figure 3B).

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: The mEGFR MAF increased to 5.6% at 13 months, and MET amplification was detected in a liquid biopsy at 15 months.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: At progression (18 months), the mEGFR MAF had increased to 20.7%, while cfChIP showed only moderate mEGFR enrichment.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: Despite the detected MET amplification, MET cfChIP enrichment remained low, with no increase relative to baseline.

body.section: 3.2. Evaluating EGFR and MET Transcription in Liquid Biopsies
body.text: The patient subsequently received crizotinib but did not respond, whereas subsequent chemotherapy resulted in a partial response, accompanied by a decrease in the mEGFR MAF to 5.2% and later 0.4%.
In this study, we investigated two patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC in whom MET amplification was detected by a liquid biopsy as a potential resistance mechanism to first-line osimertinib.
The aim was to explore whether cfChIP can provide additional information on gene transcriptional activity via serial liquid biopsies from patients treated with osimertinib.

Analysis of the serial plasma samples with cfChIP ddPCR revealed increased mEGFR and MET enrichment in PT1, who responded to crizotinib/osimertinib combination therapy, both at disease progression on osimertinib and following the initiation of combination therapy.
While mEGFR fragments were presumed exclusive to tumor cells, MET fragments can also originate from healthy cells, and the MET cfChIP signal has therefore not been established as tumor-specific.
Consequently, increased MET cfChIP enrichment cannot by itself be interpreted as increased MET transcriptional activity specifically in the tumor.
Nevertheless, in PT1, MET cfChIP enrichment increased at progression compared with baseline.

The high ctDNA fraction at baseline (54.9%) with only minor MET enrichment, followed by increased ctDNA and MET enrichment at progression, provides a case-based observation compatible with increased MET transcriptional activity occurring during disease progression, although the tumor origin of the increased MET signal cannot be established from these data alone.
In PT2, MET amplification was detected in a liquid biopsy, while MET cfChIP enrichment remained low throughout the treatment course despite an increase in the ctDNA fraction from 0.4% to 20.7%.
The MET amplification was detected in a liquid biopsy but not in the liver metastasis, and the possibility that the amplification originated from another tumor site cannot therefore be excluded.
Following crizotinib treatment, the patient did not experience a response, whereas subsequent chemotherapy resulted in a partial response and a major reduction in the ctDNA fraction.
The contrasting longitudinal observations in the two patients are of interest but do not establish a relationship between MET transcriptional activity and the response to MET inhibition.

In particular, the cfChIP-MET signal has not been shown to measure functional MET dependency, and the absence of increased MET cfChIP enrichment cannot be used to determine whether the tumor was dependent on MET signaling.

The cfChIP method reflects the overall transcriptional activity of a given gene and does not distinguish increased transcription per gene copy from increased transcription resulting from gene amplification.
In the present study, the objective was therefore to quantify the total gene-associated transcriptional activity in plasma rather than distinguish between these underlying mechanisms.
Because both mechanisms are expected to result in increased gene expression and downstream biological activity, the cfChIP results were not adjusted for gene copy number.
Previous studies have reported associations between MET-related molecular characteristics and the response to MET-directed therapies.
The phase 1b TATTON study of osimertinib in combination with the novel MET-TKI, savolitinib, indicated an increased effect in patients with MET copy number ≥ 10 in the tumor [].

In addition, another phase 1 trial evaluating the combination of the third-generation EGFR-TKI, lazertinib, and the novel bispecific EGFR/MET inhibitor, amivantamab, also demonstrated an association between treatment response and high EGFR and/or MET expression in the tumor [].
In the present study, cfChIP-ddPCR provided a minimally invasive approach for measuring EGFR and MET cfChIP enrichment longitudinally.
The biological interpretation of MET cfChIP enrichment remains challenging, particularly with respect to its tumor specificity and relationship to functional MET signaling.
The primary limitation of this study is the very small sample size, comprising only two patients with contrasting clinical trajectories.

In addition, PT1 had Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a condition associated with predisposition to multiple primary malignancies; as this patient had a prior breast cancer, it cannot be fully excluded that cfDNA signals attributed to the NSCLC were influenced by cfDNA derived from another tumor source.
The MET amplification in PT2 was detected in the liquid biopsy but not in the liver metastasis biopsy, further limiting interpretation of the origin and biological significance of the MET signal.
These limitations preclude conclusions regarding the tumor specificity or functional significance of cfChIP MET enrichment, as well as its potential clinical relevance for MET-targeted treatment.

Rather, these two cases provide hypothesis-generating observations illustrating the biological information that may be obtained by assessing gene-associated transcriptional activity longitudinally in liquid biopsies and support further investigation in appropriately powered studies.

This proof-of-concept study illustrates that, in these two patients, MET amplification did not necessarily correspond to increased MET transcriptional activity and that elevated MET transcriptional activity was observed in the patient who responded to crizotinib.

These findings provide a rationale for new prospective studies to further investigate longitudinal cfChIP-derived transcriptional activity during osimertinib/crizotinib combination therapy and establish its clinical relevance.
